topic: GROUP BY and HAVING in SQL

questions.question: What is the GROUP BY clause in SQL and how does it work?
questions.title: GROUP BY Clause in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **GROUP BY** groups rows that have the same values in specified columns into summary rows. It is used with aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG) to compute statistics per group. Every non-aggregate column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY.

interviewer_intent.testing: GROUP BY syntax and the rule about non-aggregate columns
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that all non-aggregate SELECT columns must be in GROUP BY
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the GROUP BY execution step and how it collapses multiple rows into one per group

sections.title: GROUP BY Examples
sections.content:
-- Count employees per department
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;

-- Multiple columns: group by dept AND job title
SELECT department, job_title, AVG(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department, job_title;

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- GROUP BY collapses multiple rows with same value into one summary row
- All non-aggregate columns in SELECT must be in GROUP BY clause
- Multiple GROUP BY columns: groups by unique combination of all listed columns
- GROUP BY is processed after WHERE but before HAVING and SELECT
- Can GROUP BY expressions: GROUP BY YEAR(order_date)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: GROUP BY groups rows that share the same value in the specified columns and lets you apply aggregate functions to each group. For example, GROUP BY department with COUNT star would give you one row per department showing how many employees are in each. The rule to remember: every column in your SELECT clause must either be inside an aggregate function or appear in the GROUP BY clause — otherwise the database does not know which value to show for that column. GROUP BY is processed after the WHERE clause filters rows, so you first filter individual rows, then group them.

Can you GROUP BY multiple columns?

beats.content: GROUP BY collapses multiple rows that share the same value into a single summary row. You pair it with aggregate functions to compute things per group — COUNT for totals, SUM for amounts, AVG for averages. sharp edge: every column in your SELECT must either be inside an aggregate function or appear in the GROUP BY clause. If you include a column in SELECT that is not grouped and not aggregated, the database does not know which value to show for that column when many rows collapse into one. Most databases will throw an error.

questions.question: What is the HAVING clause in SQL and when do you use it?
questions.title: HAVING Clause in SQL — Filtering Groups
questions.direct_answer: **HAVING** filters groups after GROUP BY, similar to how WHERE filters rows. Use HAVING when the filter condition involves an aggregate function. `HAVING COUNT(*) > 5` keeps only groups with more than 5 rows.

interviewer_intent.testing: HAVING clause syntax and when to use it vs WHERE
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting aggregate conditions in WHERE instead of HAVING
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that HAVING can reference aggregate functions while WHERE cannot, and give a combined WHERE+HAVING example

sections.title: HAVING Clause Examples
sections.content:
-- Departments with more than 5 employees
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

-- Combined WHERE and HAVING
SELECT department, AVG(salary)
FROM employees
WHERE status = 'active'
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 60000;

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- HAVING filters groups, WHERE filters rows
- HAVING can use aggregate functions; WHERE cannot
- Use WHERE to reduce rows before grouping (more efficient)
- Use HAVING only for aggregate conditions on groups
- HAVING without GROUP BY applies aggregate filter to the whole table as one group

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: HAVING is the GROUP BY equivalent of WHERE — it filters groups rather than rows. The key reason HAVING exists is that WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so it cannot reference aggregate functions that have not been computed yet. HAVING runs after GROUP BY and aggregation, so it can filter based on aggregate values. For example, you cannot write WHERE COUNT star greater than 5 — you would need HAVING COUNT star greater than 5. A good practice is to use both: WHERE to filter individual rows before grouping, and HAVING to filter the resulting groups.

speakable_v2.hook: HAVING exists for one reason: WHERE cannot see aggregate values — here is why that matters.

beats.content: HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY has run. It is the aggregate-aware counterpart to WHERE. WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping, and because aggregation has not happened yet at that stage, you cannot write WHERE COUNT star is greater than 5. HAVING runs after aggregation, so it can filter based on aggregate values like COUNT, SUM, and AVG.

The best practice is to use both together: WHERE reduces the rows before grouping happens, and HAVING filters the resulting groups. For example, WHERE status equals active first cuts inactive employees, then HAVING AVG(salary) greater than 60000 keeps only departments where the active employees' average salary clears that threshold.

content: HAVING without GROUP BY treats the entire table as one group
You can reference aggregate functions directly in HAVING without needing an alias

speakable_v2.cap: HAVING filters groups after aggregation — it is the only place where COUNT, SUM, and AVG conditions belong.

questions.question: What is the SQL execution order for GROUP BY queries?
questions.title: SQL Execution Order with GROUP BY and HAVING
questions.direct_answer: SQL execution order: **FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT**. WHERE runs before grouping (filters rows), HAVING runs after grouping (filters groups).

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep understanding of SQL query processing pipeline
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to use SELECT aliases in WHERE or HAVING clauses
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use this to explain all the gotchas that stem from execution order — alias usage, aggregate placement, etc.

sections.title: SQL Execution Order
sections.content:
1. **FROM** — identify tables, execute JOINs
2. **WHERE** — filter individual rows
3. **GROUP BY** — group remaining rows
4. **HAVING** — filter groups
5. **SELECT** — compute expressions, assign aliases
6. **DISTINCT** — remove duplicates
7. **ORDER BY** — sort results (can use aliases here)
8. **LIMIT/OFFSET** — return final rows

sections.title: Execution Order Example
sections.content:
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
FROM employees
WHERE status = 'active'
GROUP BY dept
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC
LIMIT 5;

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The SQL execution order is: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, and then LIMIT. This order explains several SQL behaviors. WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so it filters rows before grouping — this is why you cannot use aggregate functions in WHERE. HAVING runs after GROUP BY, which is why it can use aggregates. SELECT runs after WHERE and HAVING, which is why aliases defined in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE or HAVING. However, ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so you can reference SELECT aliases there. Understanding this order helps you write correct SQL.

followup_questions: Why can ORDER BY use SELECT aliases but WHERE cannot?
At what step do JOINs get processed?
What happens if both WHERE and HAVING are used?

seo.metaTitle: SQL Execution Order with GROUP BY and HAVING | Java Interview

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app with JPA over a relational database
speakable_v2.hook: Knowing the SQL execution order lets you reason about every clause placement question in an interview.

beats.content: The logical order SQL processes a GROUP BY query is: FROM to identify the tables, WHERE to filter individual rows, GROUP BY to group the remaining rows, HAVING to filter those groups, SELECT to compute the output columns and aliases, ORDER BY to sort, and finally LIMIT to cap the count.

This order explains three common gotchas. First, aggregate functions cannot go in WHERE because aggregation has not happened at that step. Second, SELECT aliases cannot be used in WHERE or HAVING because SELECT runs after both. Third, ORDER BY can use SELECT aliases because it runs after SELECT.

content: WHERE runs at step 2 — filters raw rows before any grouping
HAVING runs at step 4 — filters groups after aggregation
ORDER BY runs at step 6 — the only clause that can reference SELECT aliases

speakable_v2.cap: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT — knowing this order answers a dozen different SQL questions.

questions.question: How do you group by multiple columns in SQL?
questions.title: Grouping by Multiple Columns in SQL
questions.direct_answer: List multiple columns in GROUP BY separated by commas. `GROUP BY department, job_title` creates one group per unique combination of department and job title. Each unique combination becomes one row in the result.

interviewer_intent.testing: Multi-column GROUP BY syntax and combinatorial behavior
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking multi-column GROUP BY groups by each column independently
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that grouping is by unique combination and give a visual example of how rows collapse

sections.title: Multi-Column GROUP BY
sections.content:
SELECT
  department,
  YEAR(hire_date) AS hire_year,
  COUNT(*) AS hired
FROM employees
GROUP BY department, YEAR(hire_date)
ORDER BY department, hire_year;

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Multi-column GROUP BY groups by unique combinations
- (IT, 2022), (IT, 2023), (HR, 2022) are three separate groups
- Order of columns in GROUP BY matters for readability but not correctness
- All GROUP BY columns should be in SELECT for meaningful output
- Can GROUP BY expressions like YEAR(date_col)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To group by multiple columns, you list them all in the GROUP BY clause separated by commas. SQL groups by unique combinations of all the specified columns together. So GROUP BY department, job_title creates one group for each unique pair of department and job title. If you have IT engineers, IT managers, and HR engineers, you get three separate groups. This is useful for hierarchical reporting — for example, counting employees per department per year of hire.

followup_questions: How many groups would GROUP BY department, year produce for 3 departments and 4 years?
Can you GROUP BY an expression in SQL?
What is the difference between GROUP BY a, b and GROUP BY b, a?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app with JPA over a relational database
speakable_v2.hook: Multi-column GROUP BY produces combinations, not independent groups — that distinction catches people out.

beats.content: When you list multiple columns in GROUP BY, SQL creates one group for each unique combination of all of them together. GROUP BY department, job_title means IT plus Engineer is one group, IT plus Manager is a separate group, and HR plus Engineer is yet another group — even though IT appeared in two of those.

A useful real-world example: counting how many employees were hired per department per year. GROUP BY department, YEAR(hire_date) produces one row for each unique department-year pair, so you can see growth trends for each department over time.

content: The order of columns in GROUP BY does not change the groups — only the sort order if you are also ordering by them
You can GROUP BY expressions like YEAR(date_col) or MONTH(date_col), not just plain columns

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in terms of performance?
questions.title: WHERE vs HAVING Performance in SQL
questions.direct_answer: **WHERE** is more efficient because it reduces the dataset before the expensive GROUP BY and aggregation steps. HAVING processes all rows first then filters groups. Use WHERE for all non-aggregate filters.

interviewer_intent.testing: Performance understanding of WHERE vs HAVING placement
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting all filters in HAVING when some could be in WHERE for better performance
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Quantify with an example: filtering 1M rows to 10K before grouping vs grouping all 1M rows then filtering

sections.title: Performance Comparison
sections.content:
-- Less efficient: non-aggregate condition in HAVING
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM employees
GROUP BY dept
HAVING dept = 'IT';

-- More efficient: same condition in WHERE
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM employees
WHERE dept = 'IT'
GROUP BY dept;

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- WHERE runs before aggregation, reducing rows early
- HAVING runs after aggregation — more rows processed
- For 1M rows filtered to 10K: WHERE + GROUP BY processes 10K, HAVING processes 1M first
- Non-aggregate condition in HAVING is a performance antipattern
- Use WHERE for row-level conditions, HAVING only for aggregate conditions

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: WHERE is more performant for row-level filtering because it runs before GROUP BY and aggregation. If you have 1 million rows and filter to 10,000 in WHERE, the GROUP BY only has to process 10,000 rows. If you put the same condition in HAVING, the database groups all 1 million rows first, then filters. The rule of thumb is: use WHERE for any condition that does not involve aggregate functions, and reserve HAVING only for conditions that require aggregates. A non-aggregate condition in HAVING is a performance antipattern.

followup_questions: Is there any case where a non-aggregate condition belongs in HAVING?
How does the query optimizer treat conditions in WHERE vs HAVING?
What is the execution plan impact of WHERE vs HAVING?

seo.metaTitle: WHERE vs HAVING Performance in SQL | Java Interview Questions
seo.metaDescription: Understand why WHERE is more efficient than HAVING for row filtering in SQL. Java backend fresher interview question on SQL query performance.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app with JPA over a relational database
speakable_v2.hook: WHERE versus HAVING is not just a correctness question — putting the wrong condition in the wrong place costs real performance.

beats.content: WHERE runs before GROUP BY and reduces the number of rows the database has to group. HAVING runs after grouping on the already-aggregated results. If your table has one million rows and your condition cuts it to ten thousand, putting that condition in WHERE means GROUP BY only processes ten thousand rows. Putting the same condition in HAVING means the database still groups all one million rows first.
The practical rule: any condition that does not involve an aggregate function belongs in WHERE. Only conditions that reference COUNT, SUM, AVG, or similar aggregates must go in HAVING.

content: Non-aggregate condition in HAVING — like HAVING department equals IT — is a performance antipattern
WHERE can also use indexes; HAVING operates on already-processed grouped data

speakable_v2.cap: WHERE filters early and cheaply; HAVING filters late on aggregated data — never put a non-aggregate condition in HAVING.
followup_handoff: Is there any case where a non-aggregate condition belongs in HAVING?
How does the query optimizer treat conditions in WHERE vs HAVING?

questions.question: Write a SQL query to find departments with more than 3 employees earning above 50000.
questions.title: SQL Query — WHERE + GROUP BY + HAVING Combined
questions.direct_answer: Use WHERE to filter salary > 50000, GROUP BY department, then HAVING COUNT(*) > 3: `SELECT department FROM employees WHERE salary > 50000 GROUP BY department HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;`

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to combine WHERE + GROUP BY + HAVING correctly
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting both conditions in HAVING or confusing which filter goes where
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through execution steps and explain why WHERE comes before GROUP BY

sections.title: Solution
sections.content:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS high_earners
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 50000
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
ORDER BY high_earners DESC;

sections.title: Breaking Down the Query
sections.content:
- WHERE salary > 50000: row-level filter, runs before grouping
- GROUP BY department: groups the filtered employees by department
- HAVING COUNT(*) > 3: group-level filter, keeps departments with 4+ high earners
- Cannot put salary condition in HAVING: it is a row-level condition
- Cannot put COUNT(*) > 3 in WHERE: COUNT has not been computed at that stage

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: For this query, I need WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING together. First I filter individual rows with WHERE salary greater than 50000 to get only high-earning employees. Then GROUP BY department groups those employees by department. Finally HAVING COUNT star greater than 3 keeps only departments where more than 3 of those high earners work. The key insight: the salary condition must go in WHERE because it is a row-level filter before grouping. The COUNT condition must go in HAVING because it is an aggregate condition computed after grouping.

followup_questions: Why can't you put salary > 50000 in HAVING?
How would you also show the average salary for these departments?
What if you wanted departments with average salary > 50000 instead?

seo.metaTitle: SQL WHERE GROUP BY HAVING Combined Query | Java Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn to write SQL queries combining WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING clauses. Java backend fresher interview practical SQL question.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app with JPA over a relational database
speakable_v2.hook: This classic combo query — WHERE plus GROUP BY plus HAVING — shows up in almost every SQL coding round.

beats.content: Break the problem into two separate conditions: filtering individual employees by salary, and then filtering departments by headcount. The salary condition is a row-level filter — it belongs in WHERE. The headcount condition requires counting after grouping — it belongs in HAVING.

The query structure is: WHERE salary is greater than 50000 cuts down to high earners first. GROUP BY department groups those employees. HAVING COUNT star greater than 3 then keeps only departments where more than 3 of those high earners work.

content: You cannot put the salary condition in HAVING — it is not an aggregate condition
You cannot put the COUNT condition in WHERE — COUNT has not been computed at that stage
Including ORDER BY high_earners DESC at the end ranks departments by size

speakable_v2.cap: Row-level filters go in WHERE, aggregate filters go in HAVING — split the conditions and the query writes itself.
followup_handoff: Why can't you put salary > 50000 in HAVING?
What if you wanted departments with average salary > 50000 instead?
